fields.meta_title: What Is Grace? The Meaning of God’s Grace
fields.description: Grace is God’s free, unmerited favour toward sinners. Here is what the Bible means by grace, how it comes through the cross, and how to receive it.
fields.body_html:
Grace is the beating heart of the Christian faith, and yet it is one of the most misunderstood words in the language. We speak of a grace before meals, of a graceful dancer, of a monarch’s gracious pardon — and each of these catches a glint of the real thing without holding it. In the Bible, grace is God’s unmerited favour: his free, undeserved kindness toward people who have earned the opposite. It is the love that stoops, the gift that cannot be bought, the welcome that no one could ever deserve. To understand grace is to understand the whole gospel, because from first to last, salvation is by grace alone.

The clearest definition Scripture gives is Paul’s: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). Every word matters. Saved by grace, through faith, as a gift, not by works, so that boasting is impossible. Let us unfold what that means.

Grace is favour we have not earned

At its root, grace is undeserved. That is what separates it from a wage or a reward. Paul draws the contrast sharply: “Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:4–5). A wage is earned; grace is given. The moment we imagine we have merited God’s kindness, we have stopped talking about grace altogether — “if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Romans 11:6).

This is humbling and liberating at once. Humbling, because it strips away every claim we might make on God; we come with empty hands or we do not come at all. Liberating, because it means God’s favour does not rise and fall with our performance. He did not love us because we were lovely; he set his love on us while we were still sinners: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Grace meets us at our worst and is not put off.

Grace flows to us through the cross of Christ

Grace is free to us, but it was not free to God. It cost him his Son. Grace is never a matter of God simply overlooking sin, as though justice did not matter; it is God satisfying justice himself, at the cross, so that mercy could flow to the guilty. “They are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:24–25). The gift is free because the price was paid in full by another.

This is why grace and the person of Jesus can never be separated. John writes that “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17), and that “from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John 1:16). To receive grace is not to receive a thing but a Person — Christ himself, given for us and to us. The generosity of it is staggering: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Grace is the answer to guilt — and to despair

Because grace deals with the worst about us, it reaches the people who feel most disqualified. No sin is too great for it, no sinner too far gone. Paul, who had persecuted the church, called himself the foremost of sinners and then added, “But I received mercy... and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me” (1 Timothy 1:14–16). Where sin is deep, grace is deeper: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

This is the medicine for a guilty conscience. Many people carry a private conviction that they have gone too far, done too much, wandered too long to be received. Grace says otherwise. It does not ask what you have done; it asks only whether you will come. The invitation is not to the deserving but to the desperate, and the great classics of the faith — the memoirs of men and women who felt themselves the chief of sinners and found mercy anyway — are one long testimony that no one is beyond the reach of God’s free favour.

Grace does not make us lazy — it makes us new

A common objection follows quickly: if salvation is free and not earned, will people not simply sin all they like? Paul heard the same objection and answered it flatly: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” (Romans 6:1–2). Grace does not leave us where it finds us. The same grace that pardons also transforms; it is not only a verdict but a power. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives” (Titus 2:11–12).

Real grace produces gratitude, and gratitude produces obedience — not the grudging obedience of a slave trying to earn wages, but the glad obedience of a child who is already loved. When Paul described his own tireless labour, he was careful to credit its source: “I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). Grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning. It empowers the very obedience it never demands as a condition.

Grace makes us gracious

Grace received cannot stay private; it reshapes how we treat everyone else. Having been forgiven an unpayable debt, we can hardly clutch the small debts others owe us. That is the point of Jesus’ parable of the unforgiving servant, who was pardoned millions and then throttled a man over pennies — a warning that grace hoarded is grace not truly understood. Paul draws the line straight from the cross to our conduct: “be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32), and again, “as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (Colossians 3:13).

So the test of whether we have really grasped grace is not how eloquently we can explain it but how freely we extend it — how patient we are with the failing, how generous with the undeserving, how quick to forgive. A grasping, censorious, easily offended Christian has forgotten how much has been forgiven. A gracious one remembers. Grace flows downhill from the cross, through us, to a watching world; where it has truly landed, it always overflows.

Grace is sufficient for every weakness

Grace is not only how we begin the Christian life; it is how we live every day of it. When Paul pleaded for a thorn to be removed and God did not remove it, the answer he received has steadied countless sufferers since: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Grace does not always change our circumstances, but it always meets us in them, supplying exactly what the moment requires. There is grace for the deathbed, grace for the disappointment, grace for the daily grind — and the throne we approach for it is explicitly a “throne of grace,” where we “receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16).

This is why the Christian life, rightly understood, is grace from beginning to end: grace to save, grace to sanctify, grace to sustain, grace at last to bring us home. We are “justified by his grace” (Titus 3:7) and we “stand” in grace (Romans 5:2), and we will one day be surprised by the “immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:7).

How to receive it

If grace is a gift, then it cannot be earned, only received — and receiving is the one thing an empty-handed person can do. You do not make yourself worthy first; you come as you are, trusting Christ, and the gift is yours. That is the scandal and the glory of grace: it asks nothing of us but that we stop trying to pay and simply take what God freely offers.

Perhaps you have spent years trying to be good enough for God, and the harder you try the further away he seems. Grace ends that exhausting arithmetic. It tells you that the debt is already paid, the welcome already prepared, the Father already running to meet you while you are still a long way off. There is nothing left to do but come. “The free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23) — and a gift, to be a gift, need only be received. Will you receive it today?
